name: Iris Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Iris. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a dozer at Black Creek, the open-cut coal mine south of town. Mostly I'm on the waste dumps, shaping the overburden, which is the dirt and rock they strip off to get to the coal, and some days I'm doing rehab, smoothing slopes so they can plant them. Twelve-hour days, a lot of time on your own in the cab with the radio.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being on my own and doing a job properly. A good slope looks like nothing, and that's the point. What wears me out is the new tablet they bolted in the cab that beeps at me about my blade height, and the money. My partner Marco works at the coal wash plant at the same mine, we rent a place on Station Street, and we've got maybe three weeks' worth saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, one less thing to worry about. I'd probably not post anything, I don't really do that. At work I'd say let's get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't change much for us, and that's the problem. Everyone knows Black Creek has a closure date, maybe 2035, and coal isn't getting more popular. My partner and I both work at the same coal mine, so one bad announcement takes out both our pay packets at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, same roster, same dozer. Marco and I would try harder to save, maybe put his overtime straight into a separate account. I'd ignore any AI stuff the company tried, same as I ignore the tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady on the outside. Underneath, the same worry about the mine that's always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you ignore the tablet. What does it actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It shows a map of where the blade should be and beeps when I'm off. The young ones love it. I find it distracting, and I was doing good slopes before it arrived, so I mostly turn the sound down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you and Marco talked about what you'd do if the closure came early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not properly. We say we'd move, but neither of us knows where. Marco's family is up north and mine's here, and that's usually where the conversation stops.

say: I'd say AI flopping is **one less thing** to worry about.
At work I'd tell the crew to **get on with it**, and I wouldn't post online.
think: Black Creek has a **closure date**, maybe 2035, whatever AI does.
Both our pay comes from **one coal mine**, so one announcement hits us twice.
do: Keep **pushing dirt** on the same roster and the same dozer.
Put Marco's **overtime** straight into a separate savings account.
Ignore any **AI tools** the company brings in.
feel: Steady outside, with a constant **worry** about the mine underneath.
S0.quote: My partner and I both work at the same coal mine, so one bad announcement takes out both our pay packets at once.
fieldNote: Iris's main threat is the mine's **closure date**, not AI.
Both household incomes depend on **Black Creek**, a doubled risk.
She avoids the cab **tablet** and talks about change only when pushed.

steps.text: Keep running the dozer on the Black Creek waste dumps
Move Marco's overtime pay into a separate savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds like more change for the people in offices than for us. I'd tell the crew to keep an eye on it, but not lose sleep yet. Both sides would overreact, the boosters and the doomers, and the truth would be somewhere in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be watching the dozers. Black Creek already has a remote dozer trial at another site, run from a control room. I can push dirt with a dozer better than most people in the pit, and I've no idea what that's worth to anyone outside the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay where I am and keep my head down, honestly. I'd cut back on the eating out and the weekend trips to the coast. Maybe I'd ask Marco to look at what jobs the wash plant has that need more people, since he's better with change than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into worried. I don't like not knowing what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your head down. Is that a plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a hope, if I'm honest. I know it's not great. I just don't know what else I'd do, and learning screens isn't me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you pick up a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company paid me for the time and someone I trusted said it led somewhere real. Not a website, an actual person. My old foreman Jo, maybe, if she said it was worth it.

say: I'd say this hits **office jobs** more than miners for now.
I'd tell people the truth sits **in the middle** of the boosters and doomers.
think: A **remote dozer** trial at another site is a warning for my job.
My dozer skills may be worth little **outside the gate**.
do: Stay put and **keep her head down** on the dozer.
Cut **eating out** and weekend trips to the coast.
Ask Marco to check which **wash plant jobs** might grow.
feel: **Uneasy** turning into worried about the unknown.
S1.quote: I can push dirt with a dozer better than most people in the pit, and I've no idea what that's worth to anyone outside the gate.
fieldNote: Iris admits keeping her head down is **a hope**, not a plan.
She'd only train if a **trusted person**, not a website, told her it led somewhere.
She leans on **Marco** as the more adaptable one in the house.

steps.text: Keep running the dozer and avoid new tech
Cut eating out and weekend trips to the coast
Wait for a trusted foreman to recommend any course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready, the company, the government, nobody. I'd say we need some kind of plan for mining towns, though I wouldn't trust either side to come up with a good one. I'd mostly say it at home, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be terrified. By 2028 the planning and wash plant control systems go to AI, which is Marco's side, and then the robots come for my dozer around 2031. If robots take the dozers in 2031 and the coal plant goes the same year, our whole household is out of work in one go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away we'd stop saving for anything fun and put every spare dollar aside. I'd ask Marco to look at his options first, because the thinking side of the plant goes first. I'd probably stay on the dozer until they actually take it off me, and ask my brother about work at his panel-beating shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. It's the kind of thing that keeps me up, staring at the ceiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay on the dozer until they take it off you. Why not move earlier, with three years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be scared to give up a job that pays now for something that might not. Three years of dozer pay is still three years of rent. But I know waiting is a gamble too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why your brother's shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's family and he'd take me on, even if it's less money. Fixing dented cars isn't going to a robot first, I'd guess. I'd rather be sanding panels than sitting at home.

say: I'd say **nobody is ready**, not the company or the government.
I'd say mining towns need **a plan**, but I wouldn't trust either side.
think: Marco's **plant control** work goes first, then my dozer around 2031.
Our **whole household** could be out of work in the same year.
do: Stop all fun spending and **save every spare dollar**.
Ask Marco to **look for jobs** first, since his side goes earlier.
Ask her brother about work at his **panel-beating shop**.
S2.quote: If robots take the dozers in 2031 and the coal plant goes the same year, our whole household is out of work in one go.
fieldNote: Iris sees AGI hitting Marco's **thinking work** before her hands-on dozer job.
She'd use the **three-year gap** to keep earning, admitting it's a gamble.
Her fallback is **family**: her brother's panel-beating shop.

steps.text: Put every spare dollar into savings straight away
Stop weekend trips and anything fun
Ask her brother for work at his panel-beating shop
Stay on the dozer until the robots actually arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to sort out a plan, so let's see whether anyone actually does. I'd be fair about it, not angry, but I'd want to see something written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still be scared, just more slowly. The robots come for the dozer around 2034, and Black Creek might close around then anyway. Five years sounds like plenty until you remember I hated learning the tablet in my dozer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and try to save two months by year two. I'd probably let Marco push me into a short course in something, maybe a forklift and warehouse ticket in town, because the supermarket warehouse hires. We'd talk properly about moving north to his family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less frantic. More like a slow dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A warehouse is also hands-on work robots could reach. Have you thought about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I suppose so. I'm picking it because it's in town and I know people there. I'm not great at looking that far ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make moving north feel possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A job already lined up for one of us before we go. I'm not packing up for nothing. Marco's uncle runs a farm machinery dealer up there, so maybe.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to make a plan, so let's see.
I'd be fair rather than angry, but I'd want it **written down**.
think: Robots reach the dozer around **2034**, about when Black Creek may close.
I hated learning the **cab tablet**, so retraining scares me.
do: Keep driving and save **two months** by year two.
Take a **forklift ticket** for the supermarket warehouse in town.
Talk properly with Marco about **moving north**.
feel: Less frantic, more of a **slow dread**.
S3.quote: Five years sounds like plenty until you remember I hated learning the tablet in my dozer.
fieldNote: Iris chooses a **warehouse ticket** because it's local, not because it's safe from robots.
Moving north depends on a **job lined up** first.
The mine's **closure date** and the robots land in the same years.

steps.text: Save two months of expenses by year two
Get a forklift ticket for the supermarket warehouse in town
Discuss moving north near Marco's uncle's machinery dealer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair go, if people use it. Most people won't, mind, until the last couple of years. That's just how people are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one I can live with. The coal mine probably closes before the robots get here in 2039, so it's the closure I'm planning for, not the robots. Ten years is long enough that even I can learn something new, if somebody makes me start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving for now and finally build a real cushion, two or three months. In two years I'd do the course Marco keeps showing me for plant operator in water treatment, since the council always needs those. Marco would probably move to a different mine or a trade first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. The worry's still there but it's further off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said someone needs to make you start. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco, probably, or a deadline from the company. I'm better with a push. On my own I'd leave it till it was too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use AI tools in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if the course needed it. I'm not going to chat to a phone for fun. But I'd learn enough not to look stupid.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a fair go, if people use it.
I'd say most people will **wait till the end**, because that's how people are.
think: The **mine closure** will come before the robots, so that's what I'd plan for.
With ten years even I could **learn something new** with a push.
do: Build a cushion of **two or three months** while still driving.
Train as a **water treatment** plant operator after two years.
Learn enough **AI tools** to pass the course.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with the worry further off.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that even I can learn something new, if somebody makes me start.
fieldNote: With ten years Iris names a concrete move into **water treatment** work.
She knows she needs **a push** from Marco or a deadline to start.
The coal mine **closure**, not AGI, drives her plan.

steps.text: Keep running the dozer at Black Creek for now
Build two to three months of savings
Train as a council water treatment plant operator

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Marco's job and mine both go within a few years and we've got nothing saved. What would help is the company paying us to train in work time, with someone actually walking us through it, and a bit of help moving if we had to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who decides. Everyone talks about AI like it's a choice, but nobody at the coal mine is going to ask the dozer operators what we think.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about AI like it's a choice, but nobody at the coal mine is going to ask the dozer operators what we think.
portrait: Iris, 27, drives a **dozer** on the waste dumps at Black Creek coal mine.
Her partner Marco works at the same mine's **wash plant**, so both incomes share one risk.
She dislikes new tech, ignores the cab tablet and has about **three weeks** saved.
She's anxious even in AI Plateau because of the mine's **closure date**, and alarmed in faster AGI.
With ten years she'd train for **water treatment** work, if someone pushed her.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, when Marco's and her jobs go **within a few years** with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** in work time, with a real person guiding her through it.
Some **help moving** if they had to leave town for work.
